title: Chapter 55: The Vault Under the Dome, Part 1 of 5: Fenton
html:
Corin Vane went to the Memory Bourse on Midwinter night in the back of a wine cart, with another man's face on, sitting on a crate of the Duke of Marrow's best, and the whole way there he thought about his hands.
The cart was waiting in the yard behind Marrow House when Tibbs brought him round. A neat closed cart, painted dark blue, with the ship and the key on its side in gold, and a gray cob in the shafts, and a boy of fifteen in gold livery on the box, yawning. In the back, packed in straw in six wooden crates, the wine. Thirty-six bottles of Marrowmere. The forty-one. Dusty and dark and very old, each one wrapped in a twist of paper with the Duke's own seal on it.
A steward had met him at the back door. A tall thin man in black, with a gold chain round his neck and a face like a closed book. He had looked at Corin for a long moment in the light of the lantern over the door. At the long sour face. At the short pointed gray beard. At the gold livery, and the white stockings, and the black buckled shoes, and the stiff left leg, and the silver-topped stick. At the white cotton gloves.
"Fenton," the steward had said.
"Mr. Grice."
The Duke had told him the steward's name. In the letter. My steward is Grice. He has known Fenton for twenty-six years. He will know you are not Fenton the moment he sees you. He will say nothing. He has been told to say nothing, and he is the only man in my household who always does as he is told.
Mr. Grice had said nothing. He had looked at Corin a moment longer, and then he had stepped aside from the door and said, "The cart is ready. His Grace's glasses are in the small box. The decanter is in the long one. His Grace will want the first glass poured before the tenth bell, and he will not drink it." A pause. "As usual."
"As usual," said Corin, in Fenton's voice. Which was his own voice, made a little lower and a little drier, the way Vespera had told him to make it. Sour, she had said. Like you've just tasted the wine and it's corked.
And he had got up into the back of the cart, which took a long time with his leg, and sat down on a crate, and the boy on the box had clucked to the cob, and they had gone.
Now they were going down Exchange Street. Not in the line of carriages. Behind it. Down a back lane that ran parallel to the great street, behind the houses, where the tradesmen's carts went, and the coal carts, and the wine carts, and the carts of flowers and ice and cakes and fish. A narrow dark lane, full of them, nose to tail, going down at a walk toward the river. Corin could hear the cheering from Exchange Street through the houses, faint and ragged. He could see, over the roofs on his right, the glow of the torches. And ahead, at the bottom of the hill, over everything, the dome.
Lit. Glowing. Like a moon that had come down to sit on a roof.
He did not look at it. He looked at his hands.
They were in his lap. In the white cotton gloves, buttoned at the wrist. Folded, the way Fenton would fold them, sitting in the back of a cart on the way to a job he had done thirty-one times and did not much care for. They did not look like anything. They looked like a servant's hands in a servant's gloves.
Under the gloves they were gray. Dull pewter gray, from the tips of the fingers to past the wrists, going on up under the gold sleeves. Stiff. Strange. The color of a statue.
And at the bottom of the lane, at the back of the Bourse, there was a gate. The kitchen gate. A high arched gate in a high stone wall, with a lamp burning over it.
Remy had told him on Tuesday. The kitchen-gate lamp is only lit on big nights.
There was no bigger night than this.
The lane came out at the bottom into a wide cobbled space behind the Bourse. The kitchen yard. It was full of carts and light and noise. Men unloading. Boys running. Women in white aprons going in and out of a long low building with every window steaming, and the smell of roasting meat and hot fat and burnt sugar and onions coming out of it in great clouds. And in the middle of it all, at the top of three stone steps, the gate. A tall stone arch, with a pair of heavy wooden doors standing open under it, and light pouring out through them from the passage beyond. And over the arch, on a long iron hook, a lamp.
Brass. With a round glass belly. And inside the glass, a glow. Pale and greenish. Turning. Slowly. Like a fish in a bowl, looking for something.
Corin's hands began to burn before the cart had stopped.
Not ache. Not prickle. Burn. The way they had burned at the wet door, on Sunday night a week ago, when he had stood under a lamp like this one and his hands had begun to smoke and the patch of gray behind his left ear had gone up like a coal and Malakor had gone out. He felt it come up through the gloves. Into the fingers. Into the palms. Into the gray at the wrists. A deep dry heat, like holding his hands too close to a stove.
And behind his left ear, under Fenton's gray hair, the old burned patch woke up and began to sting.
He did not move. He did not take his hands out of his lap. Fenton would not. Fenton would sit on his crate, sour, and wait for the boy to get down and open the back of the cart, and then get down himself, slowly, because of the leg, and carry the first crate up the steps himself, because he did not trust boys with the Marrowmere.
That was what Fenton would do. So that was what Corin did.
The boy got down and opened the back of the cart. Corin got down. Slowly. Crutch—no. Stick. The Duke's silver-topped stick. Good foot. Swing the bad leg from the hip. And he bent, and took the handles of the first crate in his white-gloved hands, and lifted it against his chest, and turned toward the steps.
And walked toward the lamp.
Every step was worse. He felt it. The heat in his hands. Going up his arms now. Into his elbows. The sting behind his ear turning into something else, something sharp and hot like a needle pushed in and held there. He set his teeth. Fenton's teeth. Behind Fenton's sour mouth. He went up the first step. The crate was heavy. Thirty-six bottles, six to a crate. His good leg shook.
The second step.
Above him, the lamp swung on its hook. Very slightly. And the green glow inside it leaned. Toward him. The way the lamp at the palace gate had leaned on Saturday. The way a dog's head turns.
The third step.
And under the arch, in the doorway, with the light behind him, a man was standing, looking at him.
He was tall. Very tall. With a long pale face and pale hair scraped back so tight from a high forehead that it looked painted on. A gray apron. A gray shawl round his shoulders, crossed and tied, like an old woman's. And on his hands, a pair of heavy leather gloves. Smith's gloves. The kind blacksmiths wear at the forge. Too big for anything a servant would need to do. Unless what a servant needed to do was very cold.
Gorse.
Corin had never seen him. He knew him. From Oren, on Thursday night, in the crypt, with his arm in a sling, telling them about Madame Hesper's shop. A tall pale one, with his hair scraped back, and a gray shawl. He came up the stair with his bare hand. White. Smoking cold. The frost went along my sword. And from Vespera, a week ago, in the arches. Gorse looks at hands. That's what he does. He's the head of the Lady's servants and he stands at the kitchen gate and he looks at every pair of hands that comes through it.
And from somewhere much further back. From the autumn. A narrow passage behind the kitchen. A pale face bending close. Pale eyes looking down at his hands. Gorse had looked at his hands in the autumn. Tam had got him past, that time. Tam, who was dead.
Gorse looked at the crate in Corin's arms. At the ship and the key, burned into the wood. Then up. At the long sour face over it.
"Mr. Fenton," said Gorse.
His voice was soft and pale like the rest of him. Like breath on glass.
"Mr. Gorse."
"Late."
"The forty-one," said Corin, in Fenton's sour dry voice. "His Grace would have it decanted at the house. Not here. Not with your boys breathing on it."
Gorse's pale eyes did not change.
Then they went down. Off Fenton's face. Down to the crate. Down to the hands holding it. The white cotton gloves, on the rope handles of the crate. And stayed there.
Corin felt them stay there.
He felt the heat in his hands. He felt it come up through the gloves. He looked down, because Fenton would look down, to see what Gorse was looking at. And saw that the tips of the white cotton fingers, all ten of them, where they gripped the rope handles, had gone faintly brown. Like paper held too close to a candle. Just the very tips. Just a shadow. Scorching.
And a thread of something was rising off them. Very faint. Gray. Like breath on a cold morning.
The lamp on its hook over the arch swung, and leaned, and leaned.
Gorse looked at the gloves for a long time.
Then he looked up at Fenton's face again. And Corin saw nothing in the pale eyes at all. Nothing. Not suspicion. Not surprise. Just pale. The way ice is pale.
"The coal tongs, Mr. Fenton?" said Gorse softly.
Corin did not breathe.
"At the house," he said. Fenton's voice. Sour. "His Grace would have the fire in the small library made up before he left, and the boy dropped the tongs in the grate, and I picked them out." He shifted the crate in his arms, the way a man does when a crate is heavy and he is tired of being kept standing. "Thirty-one years I've carried this wine down that street, Mr. Gorse. I've burned my gloves before."
Gorse said nothing.
The lamp leaned.
And then, behind Gorse, in the passage, a woman shouted. Mr. Gorse! Mr. Gorse, the ices! A big woman, in a white apron, red-faced, with a ladle in her hand. The ice cart's at the river gate and they're saying they've no order and the Lady's ices are melting while they argue—
Gorse turned his head.
Just for a moment. Just to look.
And Corin went past him. Up the last step and under the arch and through the doorway into the passage, with the crate against his chest and his scorched gloves on the handles and his bad leg swinging. Not fast. Fenton was never fast. At Fenton's pace. Past Gorse's gray shoulder. Into the heat and the noise and the smell of roasting meat.
And as he went under the arch, under the lamp, directly under it, the burning in his hands went up into something he had no name for. White. Blinding. Like grabbing a bar of iron out of a forge.
Then he was past. And the lamp was behind him. And the burning began, very slowly, to go down.
He did not look back.
But he heard Gorse's soft pale voice behind him, in the doorway, saying to the woman with the ladle, quite calmly, Tell them the order was made on Thursday, Mrs. Pratt, and if they want it in writing they may come and see me. And then, a moment after, in exactly the same voice, to nobody, very quietly:
"Thirty-one years."
Corin went on down the passage with the Duke's wine.
He did not know if Gorse believed him. He did not know if Gorse had been fooled, or had only decided, for reasons of his own, on Midwinter night, with the ices melting, not to look any closer at a sour old cellarman's scorched gloves.
He did not know which would be worse.
Pouring
For three hours Corin Vane was furniture, and it was the strangest thing he had ever been.
He had been a harvester. A Senior Investigator. A fugitive, with his face on a poster. A coal man's lad. A dead man on a barrow. He had never been furniture. He found it was a kind of magic of its own. The kind that costs nothing and needs no rod.
He carried the six crates of Marrowmere through the kitchen passage to the servants' hall, one at a time, with his stick hooked over his arm. The servants' hall was a long low room under the great hall, with a stone floor and long tables and a fire at each end, and it was full of servants in their house colors. Thorne green, which he looked at once and then did not look at again. Langley sky blue. Ost brown. Pellow pink. And Marrow gold, his own. Three other men in gold, the Duke's footmen, who looked at him as he came in, and nodded, and looked away. Fenton. They had known Fenton for years. They did not look twice.
Nobody looked twice.
He decanted the first bottle at a side table in the corner, under a lamp, slowly, the way the Duke's letter had told him. Fenton decants by candlelight. He holds the bottle up between the candle and his eye and pours very slowly, and stops when he sees the dregs reach the neck. He has never once let the dregs into the glass. He will tell anybody who asks that it is the only thing in his life he has done perfectly. Corin did not know how to decant wine. He had never decanted anything in his life. He held the bottle up between the candle and his eye, as the letter said. And poured. Very slowly. And watched the dark line of the dregs crawl along the inside of the glass toward the neck.
And stopped.
He looked at the decanter. Pale gold. Clear as water. Not a fleck in it.
He did not know how he had done that.
Then he carried it up. Through a door at the end of the servants' hall, up a stone stair that went round and round, and through another door, low, with plum velvet over it on the far side. And into the light.
He had been in the great hall of the Bourse once before, on Tuesday night, as a lamp boy, on a ladder, in Vespera's paint, with his face turned to the wall. He had not seen it like this. Full. Five hundred people. Masks and silk and velvet and the glowing vials on their plum velvet and the chandelier turning slowly on its long chain under the dome, and the heat, and the scent, and the music. He stood in the doorway with the decanter on its tray for a moment, the way any servant stands in a doorway, to see where he is going.
And saw her.
He would not have known her face. He could not see her face. But he knew the gown. Gray silk, very plain, with a high neck and long sleeves, standing by a table of glowing vials beside a great soft mountain of a man in dove-gray. He knew the way she was standing. With her weight back on her heels. Ready to take a step back if she needed to. Your mother's way of standing, Linus Hale had said.
And a white mask, with a seed-pearl edge, and silver thread round the eyes.
He went across the room to them with his tray.
He did not hurry. Fenton did not hurry. He swung the stiff left leg from the hip, and the decanter did not move on the tray, and the people in their masks moved out of his way without looking at him, the way you move out of the way of a chair being carried. He came up beside the Duke. And said, in Fenton's sour voice, Wine, your Grace? And poured. And gave the Duke his glass. And turned, and held out the second glass to her.
She took it. And her fingers touched his. Gray kid on white cotton. Under the stem.
He felt it go into him, the way a key goes into a lock.
He tapped. Once. Twice, quick. And bowed, Fenton's sour little bow. And went away.
And then for an hour he was furniture.
He stood by the wall near the gallery stair with the tray. When the Duke lifted his glass, an inch, a signal, Corin went across and poured. The Duke never drank. The glass never needed filling. Corin filled it anyway, a drop, every time, because that was what the signal meant, the letter said. It means: I'm still here, Fenton, and so are you. And went back to the wall.
Nobody looked at him. Not once. Not the Lady's servants in plum, who went past him a hundred times with their trays. Not the Hill, in its masks. Not the woman in violet at the gallery rail, with her necklace of little lights. Not the two white masks three boxes along from hers, the slight gray one and the straight white one, who looked at everybody.
He stood by the wall and watched the room with Fenton's heavy-lidded eyes, and nobody saw him at all.
And at the ninth bell, the garden door opened.
He was facing it. That was the thing. He was standing by the wall near the gallery stair, and the garden door was on the far side of the room, to the left of the bronze doors, and when the porters drew the velvet back he was looking straight at it. He saw the small dark door in the old stone. He saw it open. He felt the cold come across the room, all the way to his wall, and bend the candles, and touch his face, Fenton's face, like a hand.
He saw Lucian come through. Counting.
He saw the two men in white.
And he saw the tall man in the black half-mask.
And his hands began to shake.
He did not notice at first. He was looking at the door. And then the decanter on the tray in his hands began to make a sound. A small thin ringing. Glass on silver. And he looked down. And the tray was shaking. And the pale gold Marrowmere in the decanter was trembling, a little ring of ripples going round and round on the surface of it. And under the tray, his hands, in their scorched white cotton gloves, were shaking so hard that he could not hold the tray still.
The way they had shaken at the railing on Saturday. On the Garden Steps. The iron humming under them.
He did not know why.
He put the tray down. On a little gilt table by the wall, very carefully, so that the decanter would not fall. And put his hands behind his back, the way servants put their hands behind their backs, and held them there, one gloved hand clamped round the other wrist. And they went on shaking. Behind his back. Where nobody could see.
The room had gone quiet.
And then everybody bowed.
Corin bowed too. Fenton bowed. Down on one knee, as the Lady's servants did, as all the servants did, on the black and white marble, with his stiff left leg out to one side because it would not bend, and his head down, and his hands behind his back, shaking.
And inside him, behind his left ear, in the room behind the door, something went very still.
Not quiet. Still. The held breath. The way it had been on Saturday at the railings. A man pressed flat against a wall in the dark while somebody walks past with a lamp.
Malakor, thought Corin.
Nothing.
And then, so faint that it was hardly more than the shape of words, a breath with a shape in it:
Don't look at him.
Corin kept his head down.
Don't look at him, boy. Look at the floor. You're a servant. Servants look at the floor. The dry old voice was so faint, so thin, like a voice from the bottom of a well. Whatever you do tonight. Whatever happens. Don't look at his face.
"He has a mask on," Corin breathed. Under his breath. Into the floor.
I know what he has on.
And then nothing. The voice went back behind the door. Still. Holding its breath.
The room straightened. Corin straightened with it. Slowly, because of the leg. He got up off his knee, with his hand on the gilt table, and stood by the wall with his hands behind his back, and looked at the floor.
He did not look at the man in the black mask. Not once. Not when the man walked across the room. Not when he sat down in the plain chair by the brass box. Not when the little gap opened in the crowd in front of him and closed behind him. Corin looked at the floor, and at the Duke's glass, and at the gray gown by the table of loves, and at the wall.
And his hands shook behind his back, all the rest of that hour, and he did not know why, and he did not look.
